llm.summary: The instructions generally match a ClawHub publishing workflow, but there are several mismatches and risky steps (undeclared env vars, root-path operations, and guidance to use proxies to bypass bot detection) that warrant caution before running anything.

dimensions.detail: Skill name/description (publish to ClawHub) aligns with most instructions (use clawhub CLI, publish/sync, semver, inspect). However the guidance to copy skills into /root/.openclaw/workspace/skills and to use BrowserBase/Camo Fox/residential proxies goes beyond a simple publish workflow and requires elevated filesystem access and external proxy tooling; those items are plausible but unusual and deserve justification.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs copying files into /root paths and changing permissions, installing an npm global package, and exporting BrowserBase-related env vars. It also explicitly advises using residential proxies/Camo Fox to bypass bot detection. The doc references env vars and external services that are not declared in the registry metadata and instructs operations that require root filesystem write/read — these broaden the skill's operational scope and risk.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the registry (instruction-only). The docs recommend `npm install -g clawhub`, which is a normal, traceable install method but still executes third-party code on the host. Because the registry metadata contains no install step, users should verify the npm 'clawhub' package source before running a global install.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Registry metadata lists no required env vars, yet the instructions require a ClawHub API token and show BrowserBase env vars (BROWSERBASE_CAMO_FOX, BROWSERBASE_PROXY_TYPE). This mismatch (undeclared creds/env vars) is inconsistent and increases the chance of accidental credential exposure or misuse. The workflow also suggests searching files for tokens and copying skill content into system locations — both raise proportionality concerns.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always-on presence or special platform privileges. However the runtime instructions expect write access to /root/.openclaw and to install global npm packages and change file permissions — actions that require elevated privileges on many systems. The skill itself does not declare or justify needing persistent elevated privileges.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Before you run any of these commands: 1) Verify the origin of the 'clawhub' npm package (check its npm page and GitHub repo) — don't blindly npm -g install unknown packages. 2) Do not run copy/chmod commands as root on a multi-tenant or production host unless you understand the impact; consider using a disposable container. 3) Treat your ClawHub API token as a secret: only give it to trusted CLIs and preferably use a token with minimal scope. 4) The SKILL.md references BrowserBase and residential proxies to bypass bot checks — that can be ethically and legally problematic; avoid setting up proxy evasion unless you understand and accept the risks. 5) Note the registry metadata declares no required env vars, yet the document needs a token and BrowserBase vars — ask the publisher for source code or homepage and for an explanation of why privileged filesystem locations and proxy tooling are necessary. If you want to proceed, run commands step-by-step in an isolated environment, inspect any installed package source, and avoid pasting secrets into scripts without review.
